title: Infra Team Wiki: GPU Fleet, Capacity Planning, CI/CD, and IaC Modules
author: Maya Chen
summary: Canonical infra team wiki covering our GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking considerations, Terraform/IaC module conventions, CI/CD and build pipelines for infra, and links to runbooks. Serves as the single-page entry for oncall, new hires, and cross-team coordination.
body:
Overview

This team wiki is the canonical reference for Redwood's infrastructure engineering practices that touch GPU fleet management, capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform / IaC modules, and CI/CD for infra changes. It consolidates runbooks, operational ownership, module conventions, rollout guidance, and links to more detailed pages.

Goals
- Provide a single place for operational runbooks and ownership for GPU capacity and infra changes.
- Standardize IaC module naming, variables, and lifecycle to reduce drift and make reviews predictable.
- Define CI/CD practices and gating for infra changes (non-disruptive, tested, and auditable).
- Document capacity safety margins, SLOs, and cost controls for GPU-backed services.

Who should use this page
- Infra engineers making changes to GPU fleet, networking, or IaC modules.
- ML/Platform engineers planning capacity requests or new GPU-backed services.
- Oncall and SRE teams running incident response and capacity triage.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-engineering team (Owner: Maya Chen)
- GPU fleet steward: Carlos Ruiz (eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity)
- IaC module owner: Aisha Patel (eng-infra/terraform-and-iac)
- CI/CD and Release owner: Ben Walker (eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build)
- Oncall escalation: see eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response runbook page

Key links (quick jump)
- GPU runbook and capacity playbook: confluence:eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- IaC & GPU guide: confluence:eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026
- CI/CD pipelines: confluence:eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/ci-cd-pipelines-infra-2025
- Network & cloud accounts: confluence:eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/basic-cloud-accounts-guide-2025

Section 1 — GPU fleet & capacity planning

1.1 Fleet composition and labels
- Node types: p4d.24xlarge (training), a100-80gb (inference heavy), a10g (inference low-cost).
- Pool naming convention: gpu-{purpose}-{region}-{tier} (examples: gpu-inference-us-west-2-prod, gpu-training-eu-central-1-batch).
- Labels/tags used for scheduling: "service", "env", "owner_team", "accelerator_type", "sku_id".

1.2 Capacity planning: formulas and safety margins
- Target headroom: production fleets maintain 20% soft headroom and 10% guaranteed buffer for autoscaling.
- Cost-aware buffer: for low-cost inference pools we allow 10% headroom with automated spillover to dedicated-burst pools.
- Capacity formula (tokens/sec basis):
  - baseline_tps_per_gpu = 4000 (tokens/sec) for a100-80gb with our runtime profile
  - required_gpus = ceil(max(peak_tps / baseline_tps_per_gpu, peak_parallel_requests / avg_batch_size) * safety_factor)
  - safety_factor = 1.2 (20%) for prod; 1.1 for staging

1.3 Autoscaling policies and thresholds
- Metric: request_queue_len (per-pool) and 95th percentile latency (token-generation-ms).
- Scale-up: trigger when 1-minute avg queue_len > 10 OR 95th latency > 300ms for 3 consecutive minutes.
- Scale-down: safe when 5-minute avg queue_len < 2 AND 95th latency < 150ms for 10 minutes.
- Max scale rate: no more than 50% of pool size per 5 minutes to avoid flapping.

1.4 Cost controls and commitment bands
- Reserved vs spot mix: critical-prod pools use 70% reserved + 30% spot; non-critical uses 0-30% reserved based on committed monthly spend.
- Monthly cost alert: budget burn rate > forecast + 10% triggers finance + infra pager.

1.5 Capacity request process
- Submit a Capacity Request ticket in Jira (infra-capacity) with: service name, expected QPS/tokens, SLO, preferred regions, retention of KV caches.
- Owner validates request within 3 business days. For urgent requests, ping #infra-ops with the ticket link and include expected start date.

Section 2 — Cloud accounts & networking basics

2.1 Account structure and roles
- Account map: root org -> mgmt (billing, shared-services) -> infra-{env}-{region} (prod/staging/qa) -> customer-specific accounts for Private deployments.
- Cross-account access: assume-role patterns with MFA and short-lived creds, using oidc federation for CI.
- IAM groups: infra-admins, infra-readonly, ci-bots, gpu-ops.

2.2 VPC and networking patterns
- VPC per environment/region with standardized CIDR allocations to avoid overlap (see CIDR table below).
- Subnet types: public (ingress LB), private (service), infra-isolated (GPU fleet & internal services).
- Peering and Transit Gateway for cross-region traffic; prefer regional routing for high-throughput GPU workloads.

2.3 Security and egress controls
- Egress firewall: all GPU fleet nodes must use NAT gateways in infra-isolated subnets; only approved egress endpoints in egress-allowlist.
- KMS/HSM: GPU nodes mount ephemeral keys via KMS for model encryption-at-rest; private deployments integrate with customer KMS.

Table: CIDR allocation (text table)
- prod-us-west-2: 10.0.0.0/16
- prod-eu-central-1: 10.1.0.0/16
- staging-us-west-2: 10.10.0.0/16
- infra-services-global: 10.100.0.0/16

Section 3 — Terraform / IaC module conventions

3.1 Repository layout and module naming
- Repo split: infra-modules (shared re-usable modules), infra-environments (per-environment stacks), infra-pipelines (CI configs & policies).
- Module naming: redwood-mod-{domain}-{resource} (examples: redwood-mod-gpu-pool, redwood-mod-vpc, redwood-mod-iam-role).

3.2 Module interface standards
- All modules MUST have: variables.tf (documented inputs), outputs.tf (explicit outputs), README.md with example usage and a minimal example.
- Inputs: avoid high-cardinality inputs (prefer maps or objects); expose common knobs only (instance_type, capacity_target, spot_percentage, tags).
- Versioning: use semver tags; breaking changes must be communicated via PR with an ADR and a migration guide.

3.3 Example module usage (snippet)
module "gpu_inference_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//modules/gpu-pool?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "gpu-inference-us-west-2-prod"
  region = "us-west-2"
  instance_type = "a100-80gb"
  capacity_target = 40
  spot_percentage = 30
  tags = {
    service = "redwood-inference"
    env     = "prod"
  }
}

3.4 State and secrets management
- Remote state: use encrypted Terraform Cloud workspaces or S3 + DynamoDB with server-side encryption (KMS).
- Secrets: never store secrets in tfvars checked into git. Use secrets manager (Vault or Secrets Manager) and reference via data sources in CI.

3.5 Testing and policy-as-code
- All module PRs require: unit tests (terratest or kitchen-terraform), static checks (tflint, tfsec), and a policy check (OPA / Sentinel) enforcing tags, encryption, and restricted instance types.

Section 4 — CI/CD and build for infra changes

4.1 Pipeline stages (policy & gate flow)
- PR -> lint & static checks -> unit tests -> plan -> policy checks -> human review -> apply (scheduled or manual).
- Blocking gates: tfsec critical findings, missing tags, or unapproved instance types will fail PR.

4.2 Git workflows and required reviewers
- Use trunk-based git with feature branches. Infra PRs touching prod workspaces require two approvers, one of whom must be a module owner.
- Changelogs: every major change must include a short CHANGELOG entry in the PR describing migration steps.

4.3 Safe apply patterns
- Production apply must be scheduled with a maintenance window and announced in #infra-announce. For GPU fleets, changes that affect >10% of capacity must go through a canary apply: target a single AZ/pool, monitor metrics for 30 minutes, then progressively apply.

4.4 CI snippets and commands
- Plan locally (recommended):
export TF_WORKSPACE=prod-us-west-2
terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-terraform-prod-us-west-2"
terraform plan -var-file=secrets.tfvars -out=tfplan
terraform show -json tfplan | jq .

- Apply via CI: CI will run ``terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan`` only after the PR passes all gates and a release window is open.

Section 5 — Runbooks and incident handling (high level)

5.1 GPU capacity incident runbook (short)
- Trigger: elevated queue_len or sustained 95th latency > 500ms.
- Immediate actions (0-10 minutes):
  1. Verify dashboards: gpu-pool latency, queue_len, pod/node CPU & memory, spot reclaim events.
  2. If spot reclaim detected: trigger reserved fallback pool (manual escalation in console or run terraform apply to scale reserved pool).
  3. If queue_len > 50 and autoscaling did not trigger: run `kubectl describe` on autoscaler, review controller logs, restart autoscaler if stuck.
  4. Post a short incident note in #infra-ops with timestamp and preliminary findings.
- Recovery (10-60 minutes):
  1. Add capacity (scale target) in increments of 10% and monitor for 10 minutes each.
  2. If latencies improve, follow canary rollback if a recent change caused the regression.
  3. If capacity cannot be added due to quota, open an urgent cloud-accounts ticket and engage cloud-ops.
- Post-incident (within 48 hours): update incident postmortem and capacity forecast; if needed, request a commit to reserved capacity.

5.2 Networking incident pointers
- If GPU nodes cannot reach model artifact store: check VPC route tables, NAT gateways, and S3 endpoint policies.
- If higher packet loss: investigate transit gateway metrics and check cross-region peering.

Section 6 — Onboarding checklist for new infra engineers
- Read: infra-team-wiki (this page), infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide, gpu capacity runbook.
- Access: request infra-admin or infra-readonly in Okta, join #infra-ops and #infra-announce.
- Hands-on: run terraform plan against a non-prod workspace, create a small module PR (example in infra-modules repo).
- Shadow: 1-week shadow with oncall rotation to observe incident response.

Appendices

A — CI/CD runbook excerpt
- Always include a short test plan in PR description explaining how you validated the change locally and any rollbacks.
- For changes that may impact latency or cost, include expected impact metrics (e.g., estimated token/sec per node, cost delta).

B — Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
- Check cloud quotas: EC2 GPU quotas per region.
- Inspect autoscaler logs and recent events: `kubectl -n infra logs deploy/gpu-autoscaler`.
- Confirm Terraform state health: Terraform Cloud workspace status or S3 + DynamoDB lock table.

C — Common terraform variables (example)
- instance_type: string
- capacity_target: number
- min_size: number
- max_size: number
- spot_percentage: number
- tags: map(string)

If you are updating this page
- Add yourself to the reviewers list, include links to any new runbooks or PRs that implement the change, and increment the version date at the top. Follow the documentation standards in eng-developer-experience/docs-site.

Footer
